parts.title: Hiring a boat
parts.context: A man books a rowing boat on a lake.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a boat hire company on a lake. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Lakeside Boat Hire, good morning.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Hello. I'd like to hire a boat for a family trip on the lake.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Certainly. I'll take your details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants a family trip, so 'family' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Tom Marshall. That's M-A-R-S-H-A-L-L.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Thank you, Mr Marshall. And which day would you like to hire the boat?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Saturday the fourteenth, if you have anything free.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Let me check. Yes, we do. How many people will there be?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Five of us, two adults and three children.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: That's fine. Our rowing boats take up to six people, while the motor boats are smaller and take only four.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Then a rowing boat, please. It's cheaper, isn't it?

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Yes, it is. And how long would you like it for?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Three hours would be enough, I think, because the children get tired.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: The price is twelve pounds an hour for a rowing boat, and we ask for a deposit of twenty pounds, which we return when the boat comes back safely.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: That's reasonable. Do we need any special equipment?

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Everyone has to wear a lifejacket, and we provide them free of charge, in all sizes.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Good. What time do we have to bring the boat back?

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: By six o'clock in the evening at the latest, because we close at half past six.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: And can we go anywhere on the lake?

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: Almost, but you mustn't go past the old bridge, because the water is deeper and faster there.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: No problem. Thank you very much.

script.speaker: clerk
script.text: You're welcome. We look forward to seeing you on Saturday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Hollins Farm Shop and Market
parts.context: The owner of a farm shop describes the site to new staff.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the owner of a farm shop describing the site to new staff. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Welcome to Hollins Farm Shop and Market. I'm Anna Hollins, and I'll tell you where everything is. Please look at the plan. You come in through the main entrance at the bottom, and the path leads straight up through the middle of the site.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Let's start at the top. At the top on the left is the butcher, where all the meat comes from our own animals. In the middle at the top is the dairy, where you can buy milk, cheese and ice cream. At the top on the right is the café, which has a terrace overlooking the fields.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: On the left, about halfway down, is the bakery. You can smell the bread from the entrance! Opposite it, on the right, is the greengrocer, with vegetables picked that morning.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Near the bottom on the left is the plant nursery, where you can buy flowers and herbs. And at the bottom on the right is the children's play area, which is fenced, so it's safe for small children.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Now, some practical information. The shop is open every day from eight until six, except on Sundays when it closes at four.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Everything we sell comes from within thirty miles of the farm, which is what makes us different from the supermarkets, and our customers like to know where their food has come from.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: The farmers' market is held on the first Saturday of every month, and it brings stalls from other farms in the area, so you'll be busy on those days.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: On Wednesdays in summer we run a tour of the farm, when children can feed the lambs. You'll be asked to help with these, and I'll explain what to do.

script.speaker: owner
script.text: Finally, a rule about dogs. Dogs are not allowed in the shop or the bakery, but they can come into the café garden. Please remind visitors politely, because some of them forget.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Planning an essay on memory
parts.context: Two students plan an essay on how reliable human memory is.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ella and Raj, planning an essay about memory. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Raj, have you started planning the memory essay yet? It's due next Friday.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Only the title. I chose 'How reliable is human memory?' because I'm fascinated by how witnesses remember crimes.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: That's a good angle, and there's a lot of research on it. How long is the essay?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Two thousand words, and the tutor said we mustn't go over by more than ten per cent.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Right. And do we have to use a minimum number of sources?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: At least eight, and at least three of them have to be journal articles, not books.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: I've found a few already. Where did you look?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I started on the university database, and then I asked the librarian, who showed me how to search by topic, which saved a lot of time.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Good idea. I'd like to start with a bit of history, but I'm not sure there's room in two thousand words.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I'd leave it out. The tutor said that she'd rather have a clear argument than a long background section.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: So how should we structure the essay? Shall I suggest an outline?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Please. I think we should begin with a short introduction that explains the aim of the essay.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Agreed. Then we need a clear definition of working memory, because the term is used differently by different writers.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Right. After that, we describe a famous experiment, such as the one by Loftus about leading questions in eyewitness accounts.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: And I'd add a case study of a patient with memory loss, to show what happens when memory fails.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Good. Then we finish with a conclusion that answers the question in the title.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Perfect. Should we include a graph of the results?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I don't think so. There's no space for it, and the bibliography doesn't count in the words, because it's separate.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Great. Shall we meet on Wednesday to compare our drafts?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Yes, in the library at two o'clock.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how human memory works
parts.context: A lecture on the stages and kinds of human memory.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how human memory works. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I'll explain how human memory works. Psychologists usually describe it as a system with three stages: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Sensory memory holds information from the senses for a very short time, less than a second for what we see, and a few seconds for what we hear. Most of this information is lost at once, unless we pay attention to it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Short-term memory is where we hold information that we are using now, such as a telephone number we've just been given. In the nineteen fifties, the psychologist George Miller showed that most people can hold about seven items at once. This is known as the magic number seven. Information lasts for about twenty seconds unless it is repeated, a process called rehearsal.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: To move information into long-term memory, we need to process it deeply. Making a link to something we already know, or giving it a meaning, helps far more than simply repeating it. Long-term memory has almost unlimited capacity, and it can last a lifetime.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There are different kinds of long-term memory. Episodic memory stores personal events, such as your last birthday, while semantic memory stores facts, such as the capital of France. Procedural memory stores skills, such as riding a bicycle, and it's remarkably durable; people who haven't ridden for years can usually still do it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why do we forget? One reason is that a memory fades with time if it isn't used. Another is interference, when new information makes it harder to recall older information. Sleep plays an important role, since during sleep the brain strengthens the memories of the day.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, some practical advice for students. Spacing your revision over several days is more effective than studying all night before an exam, and testing yourself works better than simply rereading your notes. Next week, we'll look at how attention works.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
